passage: In Ottapalam, the board exam timetable was taped to the steel almirah in Gopika's room. On Friday evening she drew a neat plan: all of history on Saturday, all of geography on Sunday. "Two days, whole syllabus," she told Arnab, whose family had moved from Kolkata and who lived across the paddy field. "I'm faster than people think." Arnab, who'd heard her say this before the half-yearly exam, said nothing. Saturday brought a power cut, a visiting aunt, and the chapter on the freedom movement, which alone took till dinner. By Sunday night she had covered four history chapters out of eleven and not opened geography. She sat staring at the timetable, honestly stunned. How could it be this slow? She had been so sure.

qa.a: The timetable was taped to the steel almirah in Gopika's room.

qa.q: Why was Gopika so stunned on Sunday night?
qa.a: She had pictured a smooth weekend where she was faster than people think, so four chapters out of eleven came as a shock.

qa.q: What could Gopika do differently before the next exam?
qa.a: She could check how long her half-yearly revision really took and spread the plan over more days, with room for power cuts and visitors.

qa.q: Why might Arnab have said nothing when he heard the plan?
qa.a: Arnab had heard the same before the half-yearly exam, so he may have doubted it but didn't want to discourage her.

The boarding school library stayed open all weekend before the Class 10 prelims, and on Friday evening Joseph taped a timetable to his desk there. Saturday: all of chemistry. Sunday: all of biology. "Easy," he told Reena, who had the desk opposite. "I'll even have Sunday night free."
"You said that before the half-yearlies," she said.
"This time I'm serious."
By Saturday lunch he was still on chapter two of chemistry, stuck on balancing equations. By Saturday night he'd finished four of twelve chapters. On Sunday afternoon, with biology untouched, he sat staring at the timetable as if it had lied to him.
"How is it already four?" he said. "I thought I'd be halfway through biology."
Reena slid her own plan across: two weeks, one subject a day, chapters crossed off. Joseph looked at it for a long time.

qa.q: How many chemistry chapters had Joseph finished by Saturday night?
qa.a: He'd finished four of twelve chapters.

qa.q: Why did Joseph feel shocked on Sunday afternoon?
qa.a: He had pictured himself finishing everything with Sunday night free, so seeing biology untouched made it feel as if the timetable had lied to him.

qa.q: What could Joseph take from Reena's plan for the next exam?
qa.a: He could plan by chapters over two weeks, as Reena did, and use his own past pace, like four chapters a day, to set a realistic target.

qa.a: Reena likely saw it coming, having heard him say the same before the half-yearlies, and chose to quietly show her plan instead of saying 'I told you so'.

Dear Kunal bhaiya,
You told me in Diwali that I plan like a movie hero. I laughed then. I'm not laughing now.
Last Friday I made a beautiful plan: the entire geography syllabus over the long weekend, three days, sixteen chapters, colour-coded. I was so excited I even decorated it with stars. I honestly believed that by Monday evening I'd be done and could watch a film.
By Saturday night I'd finished three chapters. The maps took forever. Then Mummy needed help with Nani's visit, which I hadn't counted at all. Sunday I did four more. I was shocked. I kept thinking, how? The plan looked so neat.
Then I remembered that before the unit test, the same thing happened with history.
So now I'm making a new plan with half the chapters per day and a spare day at the end. Tell me if that sounds more like a real person and less like a movie hero.
Your sister,
Bhavna

qa.a: By Saturday night she'd finished three chapters.

qa.a: She was excited by her neat, colour-coded plan and pictured everything going smoothly, so she forgot the maps, Nani's visit, and what happened before her history unit test.

qa.q: What change is Bhavna making to her plan, and why is it better?
qa.a: She is planning half the chapters per day with a spare day at the end, which fits her real pace and leaves room for surprises.

qa.q: How might Kunal bhaiya feel reading this letter?
qa.a: He might smile, since his Diwali joke about planning like a movie hero turned out true, and feel glad Bhavna is asking him for advice.

Lakshmi, you're going to finish the whole syllabus this weekend? Come, sit. Let your Kishore mama tell you something.

When I was fifteen, the Class 10 board exams were a week away. I made a beautiful timetable. Saturday: all of history and geography. Sunday: all of science. I coloured it in. I felt so organised.

By Saturday evening, I'd finished two history chapters. Two. Out of twelve. I kept stopping to check facts, and each chapter was longer than I remembered.

I was shocked. And panicked. I'd done this exact thing before the half-yearly exams and forgotten.

My father saw the timetable and said, "Plan for how long it took last time, not how long you hope."

I ended up studying late for a week. I passed, but not the way I'd hoped.

So, beta, how long did last term's revision really take you?

qa.q: How many history chapters had young Kishore finished by Saturday evening?
qa.a: Two. Out of twelve.

qa.a: Young Kishore felt shocked and panicked, having planned for a bright weekend that ignored past experience.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Kishore's story?
qa.a: His father's words about planning by how long it took last time showed that hope had replaced real experience.

qa.q: How might Kishore's father have felt seeing the coloured timetable?
qa.a: His father may have felt fond but worried, recognising the same over-hopeful plan.

"You said that before the mocks," Tarun said. "And you only did half."

She sat back, shocked. "How did it take this long?"

Tarun, dropping off wedding sweets, looked at her notebook. "You planned for the best case again."

Vidya groaned. She'd imagined every chapter going smoothly, forgetting how the mocks had actually gone. She made a new plan: two chapters a day, for seven days, with one spare.
